An idol is anything we elevate as ultimate, something we treat as sacred, untouchable, or beyond question, even when it was ever only meant to be a symbol, a tool, or a guide. It could be a person, a belief, a ritual, a nation, a feeling, or even a book. It becomes an idol not because of what it is, but because of what we let it replace. What is idolatry? Idolatry is the act of replacing truth with tradition, meaning with metaphor, or freedom with familiarity. It's when we worship the symbol instead of what it was meant to symbolize, when the image becomes more important than the insight, when loyalty overrides love, and when power disguises itself as holiness. In other words, idolatry is the practice of superstition. That's the part we missed. Idolatry was never just about statues. It was never just about gold calves or carved images. It was about confusion, confusing the means for the message, the symbol for the substance, turning reminders into replacements, turning tools into thrones. That's how it happens. A metaphor becomes a mandate, a messenger becomes a master, a ritual becomes a ruler. And suddenly what was meant to point you toward truth stands in the way of it. So before we judge the ancients for their idols of stone and silver, let's take a look at the ones we built out of culture, charisma, and conviction. Because not all idols are carved, some are crafted in our own minds.
